{"id": "6:152/q03", "question": "What is the best way to deal with the orphan's property?", "turns_on": "Whether the exception requires active growth, mere preservation, or permits particular uses; several authors combine preservation and growth.", "positions": [{"id": "6:152/q03/p1", "position": "Preserve and increase the property for the orphan, using beneficial management and investment.", "reasons": "Muqatil specifies profit; Zajjaj, Thalabi, Mawardi, Wahidi, Kashshaf, Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi, Baydawi, Nasafi, Bursevi, Alusi, Elmalili, Biqai, and others join preservation to growth. Qurtubi prefers this comprehensive reading; Jishumi and Ibn Ashur stress the child's benefit, and Asad says any use must aim at improvement. Qashani excludes waste and use for personal needs."}, {"id": "6:152/q03/p2", "position": "Trade with the property to earn profit for the orphan.", "reasons": "Mujahid, Atiyya, Said ibn Jubayr, Dahhak, and Suddi report trade; Ibn Atiyya specifies a guardian who has other means. Dahhak bars taking its profits personally; Qurtubi reports Mujahid forbidding purchase from or borrowing the estate."}, {"id": "6:152/q03/p3", "position": "Preserve the property until it can be delivered to its mature owner.", "reasons": "Kalbi and Ibn al-Saib emphasize guarding principal and handing it over at the endpoint; Tabrisī reports this as another view."}, {"id": "6:152/q03/p4", "position": "Using the orphan's animal or servant can count as permitted management.", "reasons": "Zajjaj reports the view but says the wording gives no indication of it; Abu Hayyan says the proposal avoids household mixing."}, {"id": "6:152/q03/p5", "position": "Borrowing from the orphan's estate is permitted as its best use.", "reasons": "Jishumi reports borrowing among the explanations; Abu Hayyan rejects an only-loan interpretation as inconsistent with the child's best interest; Qurtubi reports Mujahid forbidding borrowing."}]}
{"id": "6:152/q04", "question": "May a guardian use the orphan's property for personal support?", "turns_on": "Whether the guardian's need and useful management make personal consumption part of the best treatment, and whether 4:6 allows food only.", "positions": [{"id": "6:152/q04/p1", "position": "A poor guardian may take a customary reasonable amount, while a wealthy guardian abstains.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd and Ibn Abbas cite need and 4:6; Ibn Atiyya says without support the property might be neglected, and Abu Hayyan puts the allowance in trading profit. Several restrict the allowance to food, excluding clothing. Study Quran reports an alternative small amount to repay when possible."}, {"id": "6:152/q04/p2", "position": "The guardian must take nothing for himself, including profit or personal items.", "reasons": "Ikrima forbids even a cap or turban; Hasan ibn Salih and Dahhak require seeking gain entirely for the orphan, with Dahhak forbidding personal profit. Qashani rules out use for the guardian's needs."}, {"id": "6:152/q04/p3", "position": "Necessary mixing to manage the estate is allowed; mixing merely to consume it is not.", "reasons": "Al-Sha'bi distinguishes the manager's purpose. The report from Ibn Abbas describes food separation causing waste and 2:220 then permitting beneficial mixing."}]}
{"id": "6:152/q05", "question": "May the guardian buy from the orphan's estate?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:152/q05/p1", "position": "The guardian may not buy from the estate.", "reasons": "Abu Ishaq states the rule, and Qurtubi reports Mujahid forbidding purchase along with borrowing."}]}
{"id": "6:152/q06", "question": "What happened after the warning about orphan property?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:152/q06/p1", "position": "Guardians separated orphan food until leftovers spoiled, then 2:220 allowed beneficial mixing.", "reasons": "Ibn Abi Hatim transmits Ibn Abbas: God distinguished reformers from corrupters; Ibn Kathir cites Abu Dawud and describes separated food and drink after the warning at 4:10."}]}
{"id": "6:152/q07", "question": "How does the exception except the best manner work grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether the omitted feminine referent describes the manner of handling or the guardian.", "positions": [{"id": "6:152/q07/p1", "position": "It excepts the best state or act of handling, with an understood feminine noun.", "reasons": "Samin allows a circumstantial reading or an omitted verbal-noun adjective and says ahsan demands the best, not merely good. Ibn Ashur supplies state or act and cites 23:96, the idiom al-lutayya wa-allati, and Salmi's line; Alusi considers the alternative of describing the guardian's quality remote."}, {"id": "6:152/q07/p2", "position": "The guardian himself must embody the best quality.", "reasons": "Alusi mentions this analysis only to call it remote."}]}
{"id": "6:152/q08", "question": "What does until the orphan reaches maturity limit?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:152/q08/p1", "position": "It limits the implied duty to preserve the estate, which is then delivered; it does not license harmful handling afterward.", "reasons": "Zajjaj, Wahidi, Abu Hayyan, Samin, Bursevi, Alusi, and Tabatabai read the endpoint semantically. Samin says a literal endpoint to the prohibition would yield an absurd permission; Thalabi and Qurtubi expressly continue the best-treatment rule after maturity. Asad says subsequent borrowing or use needs the new owner's consent."}]}
{"id": "6:152/q09", "question": "What does ashudd mean in sense?", "turns_on": "Whether the term itself names physical vigor or the developed judgment needed in this legal context.", "positions": [{"id": "6:152/q09/p1", "position": "Developed strength, vigor, or youth at maturity.", "reasons": "Thalabi compares the height of day; Antara's shadd al-nahar line is cited by Thalabi, Jishumi, Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan, Samin, and Alusi, with another poetic line in Qurtubi. Ibn Qutayba says full youthful strength before decline; Baydawi calls it adulthood; Jawhari gives an eighteen-to-thirty span. Ibn Ashur's context concerns ability to manage property."}, {"id": "6:152/q09/p2", "position": "Mature reason, knowledge, firmness, and competence in managing assets.", "reasons": "Layth says adult knowledge and judgment; Abu al-Aliya combines understanding with bodily powers; Ibn Atiyya specifies firm financial decisions and distinguishes this from the seasoned reason of age forty in 46:15."}]}
{"id": "6:152/q10", "question": "What is the morphological form and derivation of ashudd?", "turns_on": "Whether an actual singular was heard and whether the af'al pattern can be singular; authorities also dispute its derivation from strength or rising daylight.", "positions": [{"id": "6:152/q10/p1", "position": "It is a plural of shiddah, strength or toughness.", "reasons": "Abu al-Haytham treats the feminine ending as extra before the af'ul plural; Sibawayh gives shiddah, but Jawhari objects that fa'lah normally does not form af'ul. Abu Muslim compares ni'mah/an'um. Farrā and others derive it from strength."}, {"id": "6:152/q10/p2", "position": "It is a plural of shadd, with different reported vowelings.", "reasons": "Farrā says shadd is analogically expected but unattested; Abu Ubayd cites poetry for the plural. Basrans give shudd with damma, another analysis shadd with fatha; Nasafi compares shadd/fals. Qurtubi warns that analogical singulars are not heard and cites the analogous proposed ibul for ababil, plus Abu Zayd's shada and ashadda."}, {"id": "6:152/q10/p3", "position": "It is a plural without an attested singular.", "reasons": "Farrā reports no heard singular despite analogy; Qurtubi compares the lexical dispute over forms; Abu Hayyan lists this among five analyses."}, {"id": "6:152/q10/p4", "position": "It is itself a singular form.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Anbari reports this and compares al-anuk; Abu Hayyan rejects it because af'al is not established as a singular noun pattern; Samin transmits that objection from the shaykh. Baydawi and Tabrisī note the possibility."}]}
{"id": "6:152/q11", "question": "At what point does the orphan reach ashudd here?", "turns_on": "Whether ashudd here is a fixed age, puberty, or demonstrated prudence; 4:6's marriage-age and sound-judgment test and 46:15's forty-year context are central evidence.", "positions": [{"id": "6:152/q11/p1", "position": "At puberty, with sound judgment required for delivery of property.", "reasons": "Sha'bi says moral deeds begin to be recorded then; Rabi'a cites the marriage-age test in 4:6. Zajjaj, Ibn Atiyya, Tabrisī, Razi, Qurtubi, Bursevi, Alusi, Tabatabai, and others require prudent judgment too. Ibn Atiyya prefers Malik's puberty plus absence of foolishness; Tabrisī prefers no fixed age. Zajjaj rejects eighteen if puberty and judgment arrive earlier; Ibn al-Jawzi prefers puberty and doubts that older age reports belong to this verse. Alusi refers readers to his earlier treatment of the disputed handover age."}, {"id": "6:152/q11/p2", "position": "At eighteen years, or a range beginning at eighteen and reaching thirty.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Said ibn Jubayr, and Ali ibn Isa give eighteen; Kalbi and a report from Ibn Abbas give eighteen to thirty. Zajjaj objects because an earlier prudent adult must receive property."}, {"id": "6:152/q11/p3", "position": "At thirty years.", "reasons": "Suddi gives thirty; Thalabi says he then distinguishes marriageable age. Ibn Kathir considers thirty remote here; Ibn al-Jawzi suspects age reports were imported from 12:22."}, {"id": "6:152/q11/p4", "position": "At thirty-three years.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and Qatada are reported for this age; another Ibn Abbas report is transmitted by Ibn Jubayr."}, {"id": "6:152/q11/p5", "position": "At twenty-five years.", "reasons": "Ikrima gives twenty-five, and Abu Hanifa sets handover then unless mental deficiency appears. Ibn al-Arabi objects that Abu Hanifa uses weak reports to fix an age while rejecting analogical fixed measures."}, {"i

{"id": "6:152/q12", "question": "When must the guardian hand over the orphan's property?", "turns_on": "Whether 4:6 supplies a further prudence condition to this verse's maturity endpoint.", "positions": [{"id": "6:152/q12/p1", "position": "At adulthood together with sound judgment; the property is then delivered.", "reasons": "Zajjaj, Wahidi, Jishumi, Ibn Atiyya, Tabrisī, Qurtubi, and Tabatabai appeal to 4:6; Qurtubi warns that an imprudent adult may squander it. Ibn al-Jawzi says the judgment and Islam qualifications come from another verse, limiting this verse's unqualified wording. Islahi adds delivery with witnesses."}, {"id": "6:152/q12/p2", "position": "At puberty, with delivery implied directly by the endpoint.", "reasons": "Nasafi states delivery at puberty; the separate debate over required financial prudence turns on 4:6."}]}
{"id": "6:152/q13", "question": "Was the orphan maturity limit abrogated by 4:6?", "turns_on": "Whether the later testing and marriage-age instruction replaces the earlier threshold or explains it.", "positions": [{"id": "6:152/q13/p1", "position": "Yes, the later marriage-age and testing verse replaced this limit.", "reasons": "Suddi's thirty-year report is coupled with this suggestion by Ibn al-Jawzi and Tabrisī; Alusi reports the same view."}, {"id": "6:152/q13/p2", "position": "The verses are read together: 4:6 clarifies maturity by adding sound judgment.", "reasons": "Zajjaj, Qurtubi, Tabrisī, Tabatabai, and others apply both conditions; Ibn al-Jawzi frames it as qualifying an unrestricted statement rather than deriving all details from this verse alone."}]}
{"id": "6:152/q14", "question": "What do kayl and mizan name here?", "turns_on": "Whether an omitted measured or weighed noun is necessary, or kayl can directly denote the vessel or amount.", "positions": [{"id": "6:152/q14/p1", "position": "The measured amount and weighed amount, with measure also able to name its vessel and mizan the scale.", "reasons": "Wahidi says wafā means completion, kayl can imply a vessel, and mizan names weighing on the scale; Samin derives mizan from weighing on the mif'al pattern, underlying mawzan changing like miqat. Ibn Ashur names dates and raisins sold by measure and gold and silver by weight; Alusi allows the commodity sense."}, {"id": "6:152/q14/p2", "position": "They are verbal nouns standing for measured goods or acts of measuring, with supplied nouns.", "reasons": "Abu al-Baqa proposes omitted nouns; Wahidi proposes an understood weight with mizan. Samin rejects unnecessary substitution because kayl itself can name the vessel; Alusi still allows an omitted noun."}]}
{"id": "6:152/q15", "question": "What does fair fulfillment of measure and weight require?", "turns_on": "Whether fairness means exact equality without extra or a small excess to guarantee no deficit.", "positions": [{"id": "6:152/q15/p1", "position": "Give and take the full due accurately, without shortchanging or demanding excess.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas and many commentators gloss qist as justice. Wahidi defines wafā as completing without shortfall; Razi, Thalabi, Baghawi, Bursevi, and Alusi apply equity to seller and buyer alike. Ibn Kathir cites 83:1-6 and destruction for fraudulent scales. Islahi links honest measures to a just economy and 17:35; Elmalili generalizes protection of others' rights."}, {"id": "6:152/q15/p2", "position": "Slightly over-measure to ensure that the due is certainly fulfilled.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan reports this recommendation and a report instructing an added weight; he also glosses qist as exact balance."}]}
{"id": "6:152/q16", "question": "How is with fairness attached grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether the prepositional phrase qualifies the doer or the object of fulfillment.", "positions": [{"id": "6:152/q16/p1", "position": "It describes the measurer's just action.", "reasons": "Samin and Abu al-Baqa allow the agent reading; Bursevi takes it as the state of fulfillment, and Ibn Ashur says the preposition directs just conduct."}, {"id": "6:152/q16/p2", "position": "It describes the measures or measured objects as complete and fair.", "reasons": "Samin and Abu al-Baqa report the object reading."}]}
{"id": "6:152/q17", "question": "Why is the measure duty phrased as a positive command?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:152/q17/p1", "position": "It urges active justice and implies the prohibition of cheating.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur contrasts Shuayb's prohibition at 11:84 and says the command confronts Arabs who boasted of generosity while shorting buyers. Islahi compares 83:1-3; Biqai says full equity rules out merely coming close; Bursevi says the apparent repetition spells out both seller and buyer duties."}]}
{"id": "6:152/q18", "question": "What does the capacity clause qualify and excuse?", "turns_on": "Whether the intervening sentence is limited by the immediately preceding exact-measure command or extends to all nearby duties.", "positions": [{"id": "6:152/q18/p1", "position": "It qualifies measuring and weighing: reasonable care is required, unavoidable minute error is excused.", "reasons": "Mawardi, Kashshaf, Qurtubi, Razi, Ibn Atiyya, Tabrisī, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Ashur, Asad, and many others say microscopic exactness is impossible. Ibn Kathir cites Said ibn al-Musayyib's sincere-measure report as rare and disconnected; Bursevi says deliberate fraud is not excused. Ibn Ashur says the concession keeps fear of error from stopping trade. Itqan cites a weak mursal report from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib that an honest person who voluntarily exceeds a measure or weight is not blamed, applying the capacity clause to sincere measuring."}, {"id": "6:152/q18/p2", "position": "It states generally that all the listed obligations lie within human ability.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas compares 22:78; Sufyan identifies capacity with performing duties. Farisi, Jishumi, Abu Hayyan, Alusi, Ibn Ashur, Tabatabai, Islahi, and Study Quran permit the broader scope; Ibn Ashur cites 2:286 and Study Quran gives 2:286, 7:42, 23:62, 65:7. Islahi rejects both scrupulous excess and self-set limits of obedience."}]}
{"id": "6:152/q19", "question": "What does wus' or capacity mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether capacity is ordinary ability, one's own action, or performance of duties.", "positions": [{"id": "6:152/q19/p1", "position": "One's ability or what one can bear.", "reasons": "Said ibn Jubayr glosses it as ability; Ibn Abbas says obligations are manageable, citing 22:78; Ibn Kathir and later commentators apply this to honest effort."}, {"id": "6:152/q19/p2", "position": "What a person has done for himself.", "reasons": "Ibn Abi Hatim transmits this gloss from Sha'bi."}, {"id": "6:152/q19/p3", "position": "Performing the assigned obligations.", "reasons": "Ibn Abi Hatim transmits this gloss from Sufyan."}]}
{"id": "6:152/q20", "question": "What does the capacity clause imply about obliging an incapable unbeliever?", "turns_on": "Whether the easing of an attainable measurement task proves a broader rule against the disputed obligation to believe.", "positions": [{"id": "6:152/q20/p1", "position": "God cannot oblige faith from someone incapable while creating and willing that person's disbelief.", "reasons": "Al-Qadi argues from the easing of exact measurement: if the attainable task is eased, such an impossible obligation would be incoherent."}, {"id": "6:152/q20/p2", "position": "The objection fails when divine knowledge and the motive are considered.", "reasons": "Razi gives this reply to al-Qadi and his teachers."}]}

{"id": "6:152/q23", "question": "What speech does the command to be just cover?", "turns_on": "Whether the unqualified word speech is universal or primarily refers to testimony and adjudication because of the kin clause.", "positions": [{"id": "6:152/q23/p1", "position": "All consequential speech must be truthful and fair, including testimony, judgment, advice, preaching, reports, and mediation.", "reasons": "Jishumi lists wills, legal opinions, rulings, and schools; Qadi adds concise comprehensible preaching, restrained enjoining of right, accurate narratives and message transmission. Abu Hayyan rejects restriction without evidence. Tabrisī says habitual just speech also leads to just action."}, {"id": "6:152/q23/p2", "position": "Its primary application is testimony or judgment, especially in disputes involving kin.", "reasons": "Razi reports commentators' restriction to testimony or commands and prohibitions; Asad prefers an evidentiary setting because kin are mentioned. {"id": "6:152/q26", "question": "Who is the relative in even if a relative?", "turns_on": "Which omitted person is supplied as the subject of kāna.", "positions": [{"id": "6:152/q26/p1", "position": "The person spoken about, testified for or against, or judged may be the speaker's relative.", "reasons": "Wahidi reports Zajjaj's explanation that the omitted party may be beneficiary or accused, comparing 5:106. {"id": "6:152/q27", "question": "How is even if he is a relative parsed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:152/q27/p1", "position": "Dha qurba is the predicate of kana, whose subject is omitted; the waw is circumstantial and law concessive.", "reasons": "Jishumi gives the predicate analysis; Ibn Ashur explains the concessive circumstantial construction and its emphasis on the exceptional kin case; Thalabi and Wahidi explain the omitted party."}]}
{"id": "6:152/q28", "question": "What inward discipline is read in just speech?", "turns_on": "Whether the spiritual emphasis falls on God-oriented speech itself or prior correction of the speaker.", "positions": [{"id": "6:152/q28/p1", "position": "True speech is of, through, and for God, free of self-interest, and should be sparse and grounded in knowledge.", "reasons": "Tustari distinguishes God-directed speech from self-directed speech, warns that evil suspicion, irrelevant talk, and misuse of limbs destroy certainty, truthfulness, and scruple. {"id": "6:152/q29", "question": "What is God's covenant that must be fulfilled?", "turns_on": "Whether the genitive identifies a covenant imposed by God, made to God, or protected by God; the broad reading includes these together.", "positions": [{"id": "6:152/q29/p1", "position": "It embraces God's commands and prohibitions together with lawful vows, oaths, and human agreements He orders people to keep.", "reasons": "Jishumi says all senses are intended; Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan, Bursevi, Elmalili, Ibn Ashur, Islahi, and Kuran Yolu include obligations and valid pledges. Nasafi also lists promise and threat. Ibn Ashur includes polytheists' alliances and peace pacts, Arab poetry praising fidelity, Meccan Hilf al-Fudul and Mutayyibin pacts, and violation of Mecca's safety promise to Abraham. Razi stresses secret oaths can be broken unseen; Biqai includes what one owes or is owed."}, {"id": "6:152/q29/p2", "position": "It chiefly means the religious duties and ordinances God imposed.", "reasons": "Maturidi, Ibn Jarir, and Study Quran identify commands and prohibitions; Ibn Kathir adds God's Book and the Messenger's Sunnah. Tabatabai prefers this in context, citing 17:34 and 5:106, but allows a pledge to God. Baydawi names justice and religious law."}, {"id": "6:152/q29/p3", "position": "It is a vow, oath, or pledge made to God or sworn by God's name.", "reasons": "Said ibn Jubayr cites confirmed vows and 16:91; Nahhas mentions covenants with God or oaths to people; Mawardi excludes sinful oaths. Razi notes private oath fidelity is subtle."}, {"id": "6:152/q29/p4", "position": "It is the primordial covenant.", "reasons": "Nasafi lists it; Tabrizi places it on the Day of the Covenant. Qashani and Bursevi draw inward implications from it."}]}
{"id": "6:152/q30", "question": "How can the genitive God's covenant be understood?", "turns_on": "Whether God makes the covenant, receives the pledge, or authorizes a covenant between people.", "positions": [{"id": "6:152/q30/p1", "position": "God is the covenanting subject, imposing obligations on people.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and Samin explain this possessive relation; Samin cites 33:23 and 48:10."}, {"id": "6:152/q30/p2", "position": "God is the object: people pledge to Him.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan, Samin, and Ibn Ashur allow this analysis; Samin cites 33:23 and 48:10."}, {"id": "6:152/q30/p3", "position": "The attribution explains that God commands keeping human covenants.", "reasons": "Samin calls this an explanatory possessive; Abu Hayyan and Ibn Ashur also permit human-to-human covenants under God's command."}]}
{"id": "6:152/q31", "question": "Why is God's covenant placed first in its clause?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:152/q31/p1", "position": "Fronting emphasizes special priority for fidelity to God's covenant.", "reasons": "Alusi says the fronted phrase emphasizes it; Ibn Ashur appeals to an audience proud of pacts and contrasts 2:217: they should keep their chosen covenant with God. {"id": "6:152/q35", "question": "Why does this group end with remembrance rather than understanding?", "turns_on": "Whether the ending reflects complexity, familiar but forgotten virtues, or the different form of prohibitions and commands.", "positions": [{"id": "6:152/q35/p1", "position": "The first five duties are obvious, while these four need reflection to find a just balance.", "reasons": "Razi gives this explanation, followed by Abu Hayyan, Samin, and Alusi; Tabatabai says remembering social harm to weak persons, commerce, and truth demands reflection."}, {"id": "6:152/q35/p2", "position": "The audience already practiced and praised these duties but might forget them.", "reasons": "Qutb al-Razi contrasts heedless violation of the first set; he explains parents' place in the first set by their unique favor after God. {"id": "6:152/q36", "question": "How is tadhakkarun read?", "turns_on": "Assimilation of the second ta into dhal versus deletion of a ta for ease; reports differ over the deleted ta and related readings elsewhere.", "positions": [{"id": "6:152/q36/p1", "position": "It is read with a doubled dhal through assimilation of the underlying tatadhakkarun.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr double related forms throughout; Nafi, Abu Bakr from Asim, and Ibn Amir generally do so but lighten 19:67. Qiraat-ER says the heavier sound may echo active remembrance; meaning stays the same."}, {"id": "6:152/q36/p2", "position": "It is read with a light dhal by deleting one ta from tatadhakkarun.", "reasons": "Hamza, Kisai, Hafs, and in later listing Khalaf use the light form; traditions disagree over which ta is omitted. {"id": "6:152/q37", "question": "What are the form and sense of the remembrance verb?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:152/q37/p1", "position": "It is a responsive or reflexive form meaning repeated recollection or taking heed.", "reasons": "Wahidi calls tadhakkur repeated remembering; Farisi reports Sibawayh that simple dhakara takes one object, doubled dhakkara two, and Form V is its responsive form, citing Qur'an and poetry. Farisi also surveys iddikar, dhikra, the plural al-dhikr, assimilated dal pronunciation, and transitive Form VIII, citing 73:8, 12:45, 54:15, 11:54; he compares grateful recollection in 8:26 and 7:86."}]}
{"id": "6:152/q38", "question": "How are these commands connected to the surrounding passage?", "turns_on": "Whether the connected sequence is explained chiefly as public duties or as a scheme of inward virtues.", "positions": [{"id": "6:152/q38/p1", "position": "They form the second group of linked divine duties, dealing especially with interpersonal, economic, and civic order.", "reasons": "Razi counts five clearer duties in the previous verse and four subtler here. Biqai says three groups each close with a testament and progress from reason to remembrance to taqwa; Ibn Ashur describes social, interpersonal, and straight-path sections, each closed by a repeated charge. Islahi ties them to Abraham's religion against Quraysh's invented food taboos and compares 17:22-38 and 16:90; Kuran Yolu counts nine main commands and a final encompassing straight-path duty. Kashshaf and Islahi say positive and negative forms imply their opposites. Ibn Ashur begins the second group with vulnerable property and mutual trust; Islahi says justice marks Abrahamic and Islamic conduct. Samarrai links the ordering to the preceding mention of poverty, which makes short measure especially tempting, and sees the move from fair material transactions to just speech as a shift between forms of justice."}, {"id": "6:152/q38/p2", "position": "The sequence is an inward scheme of vices, virtues, and the comprehensive virtue of justice.", "reasons": "Qashani says three vice classes entail injustice, while virtues entail justice; four listed vices are followed by four corresponding virtues. He calls the balanced middle difficult and encompassing all vice and virtue. Bursevi reads lifetime and divine rights as inward measure and scale, supported by a Persian verse about each person's wings and strength."}]}

{"id": "6:153/q01", "question": "How is the opening particle of 'and this is My path' read?", "turns_on": "The transmitted vowels and nūn forms alter whether the clause can be attached to what precedes or opens independently.", "positions": [{"id": "6:153/q01/p1", "position": "With open hamza and doubled nūn.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid, al-Fārisī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Nashr, and Ibn ʿĀshūr assign it to most readers, including Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim, and Abū ʿAmr; Ibn ʿĀshūr also names Abū Jaʿfar. Al-Ālūsī also rehearses this tripartite reading as part of the preceding command's syntax."}, {"id": "6:153/q01/p2", "position": "With open hamza and light or quiescent nūn.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀmir is named throughout; several sources add Yaʿqūb, while al-Qurṭubī adds Ibn Abī Isḥāq. Sources differ whether the light particle is reduced emphatic inna or maṣdariyya."}, {"id": "6:153/q01/p3", "position": "With kasra and doubled nūn, beginning a fresh assertion.", "reasons": "Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī are consistently named; al-Aʿmash, ʿAlī and Khalaf also appear in some reports. Al-Biqāʿī instead attributes a light kasra reading to Ibn ʿĀmir and Yaʿqūb."}, {"id": "6:153/q01/p4", "position": "With kasra and light nūn.", "reasons": "Jishumī attributes this form to Ibn ʿĀmir and Yaʿqūb; al-Biqāʿī likewise reports kasra for them, against the usual fatḥa attribution."}, {"id": "6:153/q01/p5", "position": "Without the particle: 'and this is My path'.", "reasons": "Al-Aʿmash and the codex of Ibn Masʿūd/ʿAbd Allāh are reported; al-Samīn says it supports the independent-sentence analysis."}]}
{"id": "6:153/q02", "question": "What syntactic relation does 'and this is My path' have to its context?", "turns_on": "The open or closed particle, an implied causal lām, and the point of coordination with 6:151 decide the parse.", "positions": [{"id": "6:153/q02/p1", "position": "It gives the reason for the command: follow it because it is straight.", "reasons": "Al-Khalīl, Sībawayh, Abū ʿAlī, al-Zamakhsharī and others supply a causal lām. Comparisons include 106:1, 23:52 and 72:18. Al-Fārisī and Abū Ḥayyān discuss whether the following fāʾ would then be extra; al-Samīn says Sībawayh disallows that predicate fāʾ. Al-Ālūsī answers a double-conjunction objection by a fronted object or an omitted verb, citing 17:110 and 72:18."}, {"id": "6:153/q02/p2", "position": "It is an object of 'I recite': I recite that this is My path.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, al-Kisāʾī, Abū al-Baqāʾ and Ibn ʿĀshūr connect it to the recitation beginning at 6:151; al-Ālūsī calls coordination with 'come' very unlikely."}, {"id": "6:153/q02/p3", "position": "It coordinates with the earlier divine prohibition, charge, or its prepositional object.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ makes it genitive after the charge and coordinates with bihi; al-Ḥawfī attaches it to an lā tushrikū; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī attach it to the prior prohibition. Abū al-Baqāʾ objects that the preposition must be repeated and that God would be commanding the path's straightness; al-Samīn replies that the preposition can be understood after a long clause and that commanding its straightness means forbidding departure."}, {"id": "6:153/q02/p4", "position": "With kasra, it is a fresh sentence, and the following fāʾ links the command.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās, Abū ʿAlī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, and others read it as an independent declaration; the kasra still gives a reason to follow. Some connect the assertion to the Prophet's recitation."}, {"id": "6:153/q02/p5", "position": "The light form has an implicit pronoun of the matter.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAlī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabrisī and al-Samīn explain the omitted pronoun by al-Aʿshā's poetry and other examples, including 10:10. Al-Naḥḥās allows nominative or accusative; Qirāʾāt-Er instead calls the light particle maṣdariyya."}, {"id": "6:153/q02/p6", "position": "The previous explanatory construction is itself disputed.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says a nominalizing 'that you do not associate' appears to name nonassociation among forbidden things, while an explanatory particle strains to include later positive commands. He rejects a relative-clause solution ascribed to Sībawayh. Al-Zamakhsharī implies prohibitions opposite the positive commands; Abū Ḥayyān supplies an omitted 'what He commanded' or coordinates with 'I recite.' Imruʾ al-Qays's line permits an imperative beside a prohibition."}]}
{"id": "6:153/q03", "question": "How is the consonant of ṣirāṭī pronounced?", "turns_on": "The transmitted dialectal or phonological form of the initial consonant.", "positions": [{"id": "6:153/q03/p1", "position": "With ṣād.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid and later readers make it the reading of those other than the named sīn and intermediate-sound readers."}, {"id": "6:153/q03/p2", "position": "With sīn, sirāṭī.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr and Ibn ʿĀmir are named; Qirāʾāt-Er specifies Qunbul from Ibn Kathīr and calls it a phonological variant of the same root."}, {"id": "6:153/q03/p3", "position": "With an intermediate ṣād–zāy sound.", "reasons": "Ḥamza's form has variant transmissions in Ibn Mujāhid; Qirāʾāt-Er names Khalaf from Ḥamza and describes ishmām of zāy."}]}
{"id": "6:153/q04", "question": "How is the possessive yāʾ of ṣirāṭī read?", "turns_on": "Transmission of the possessive yāʾ vowel, with the same sense in both readings.", "positions": [{"id": "6:153/q04/p1", "position": "The yāʾ is quiescent.", "reasons": "Most readers leave it still. Ibn Mujāhid also gives his moving yāʾ in maḥyāy and wajhī; al-Nashr and Qirāʾāt-Er specify fatḥa, with no change in meaning."}]}
{"id": "6:153/q05", "question": "What does 'this, My straight path' designate?", "turns_on": "The demonstrative's scope ranges from immediately preceding laws to Islam and the entire sūra; inward or imamic applications identify a particular way of traversing it.", "positions": [{"id": "6:153/q05/p1", "position": "Islam, God's upright religion, including Muhammad's revealed law and Sunnah.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Dāmghānī, al-Qurṭubī and others identify it with the religion; al-Dāmghānī cites 6:126, Ibn ʿĀshūr 1:6 and 6:161, and Study Quran 5:15–16. Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers the whole prophetic law to al-Ṭabarī's narrower commandments."}, {"id": "6:153/q05/p2", "position": "The commands and prohibitions in the two preceding verses, or all ten duties.", "reasons": "Muqātil is cited for this; al-Rāzī says these summarize the entire prophetic teaching. Al-Ālūsī distinguishes the source and calls the straight path comprehensive. Elmalılı includes preceding tawḥīd; Kur'an Yolu calls the final duty encompassing."}, {"id": "6:153/q05/p3", "position": "The Qurʾān, revelation, or proofs.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī and Ibn al-Jawzī record Qurʾān as an alternative to law or Islam. Jishumī adds proofs and the absence of contradiction; al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī stress following revelation and proof. Al-Burhān includes 'the straight path' among a catalog of names or descriptions of the Qurʾān, alongside revelation, spirit, inspiration, the decisive word, the great news, and the best discourse."}, {"id": "6:153/q05/p4", "position": "The whole sūra, especially its tawḥīd, prophecy and law.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī report this scope; al-Bursawī uses the sūra's content to explain the causal clause."}, {"id": "6:153/q05/p5", "position": "Abraham's upright monotheistic religion restored by Muhammad.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās calls it the ḥanīf religion and best religion. Iṣlāḥī links it to Abraham's basic teaching, Moses' law, Quraysh's neglected moral duties and Muhammad's restoration after Israelite and Ishmaelite innovations."}, {"id": "6:153/q05/p6", "position": "The divinely guided Imams, particularly ʿAlī, as an application.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī labels Abū Jaʿfar's identification an application; reports through Shiʿi and Sunni routes name ʿAlī. He connects kinship-love in 42:23 to seeking a way to the Lord in 25:57."}, {"id": "6:153/q05/p7", "position": "The heart's route to God, without the self's desire or share.", "reasons": "Jaʿfar b. Muḥammad speaks of turning from everything other than God; Sahl excludes the self's desire. Al-Qāshānī describes balanced virtues, unity, annihilation and subsistence through divine attributes."}, {"id": "6:153/q05/p8", "position": "Every path ultimately begins from God and turns to Him.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī cites a Persian tafsīr, Qūnawī's account of God's encompassing existence or knowledge, and a Persian verse that every road crosses the Beloved's street."}]}

{"id": "6:153/q07", "question": "What does calling the way a straight path convey?", "turns_on": "The road image explains directness, destination, and contrast with branching deviation.", "positions": [{"id": "6:153/q07/p1", "position": "A clear, broad, direct road to Paradise and well-being, free of crookedness.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī and al-Bursawī explain the path metaphor by its destination; Jishumī contrasts Satan's route to Hell. {"id": "6:153/q09", "question": "What does following the path require?", "turns_on": "The sources develop following as practical obedience and adherence to transmitted communal guidance.", "positions": [{"id": "6:153/q09/p1", "position": "Act on the full revealed way, its commands, prohibitions, permissions and restraints.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī defines following as acting; Jishumī adds affirmation and lawful/unlawful observance; Abū Ḥayyān includes all obligations.
